claims.claim: A forum reader names the opening boxed text of the Dragonlance series as his favourite worst offender and quotes its first clause.
claims.source: forum member 'delericho', reply on EN World
claims.quote: The air surges fierce and sweet

claims.claim: A forum reader treats a passage in The Forest Oracle as the standing example of infamously bad boxed text, describing men who are neither tarrying nor running.
claims.quote: the men who are neither tarrying nor running

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's composition rule for a keyed location is that it must not be a single thing.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: avoid having rooms that are just one thing
claims.page: Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms

claims.claim: He puts a number on it: at least three things in the room that reward more than looking.
claims.quote: include at least three interactive elements
claims.page: Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms

claims.claim: Alexander's empty rooms still carry one flavourful feature that leads nowhere, which he distinguishes from barren and featureless.
claims.quote: commonly feature one flavorful thing which does not have a significant interaction

claims.claim: Alexander's habitual repair when prepping a published module is to flag details that are essential but buried mid-paragraph so they are not missed in play.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'How to Prep a Module – Part 2', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: essential to the adventure but buried in the middle of a paragraph

claims.claim: Reviewing the 2025 D&D starter set, Alexander finds one action defined differently in the main text and in the glossary of the same book.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, review of Heroes of the Borderlands, The Alexandrian
claims.quote: In the glossary, however, the Influence action is defined

claims.claim: An EN World poster in 2025 recalls a two-sentence ceiling for boxed text and would restrict it to what a character physically senses on entering, plus any creatures.
claims.source: EN World member 'GM Lent', post of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences

claims.claim: Another poster in the same thread sets the limit at three to five sentences, with further detail held back for players who look closer.
claims.source: EN World moderator emeritus 'el-remmen', post of 5 April 2025

claims.claim: A poster in the same thread argues for read-aloud prose against the bullet-keyword alternative, saying flat descriptors and boxes of key terms are what he dislikes.
claims.source: EN World member 'Shardstone', post of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: I really hate adventures that have very plain descriptors

claims.claim: A poster prefers vague relative placement in room descriptions over compass directions the characters may not know; another replies that vague placement breaks when the party enters by a different door.
claims.source: EN World members 'Shiroiken' and 'Lanefan', posts of 5 April 2025
claims.quote: I personally dislike the cardinal directions

claims.claim: A poster reports his players want the creatures named before the furnishings, with minor detail held until after the encounter.
claims.source: EN World member 'DragonLancer', quoted at post #39
claims.quote: never mention any monsters or at the very least

claims.claim: A poster avoids read-aloud text because module prose differs from his own speech, so reading it signals to players that the location matters to the plot.
claims.source: EN World member 'humble minion', post of 12 July 2020
claims.quote: the way modules are written is very different

claims.claim: The thread's opening poster, writing from eastern Europe, says reading published text aloud makes the DM sound like a speech synthesiser.
claims.source: EN World member 'oriaxx77', post of 12 July 2020
claims.quote: it turns the DM into a TextToSpeech bot

claims.claim: Prince of Nothing says T1's village text is split into common information and bold text the players are not meant to know.
claims.source: Prince of Nothing, Age of Dusk blog, 2021
claims.quote: divided between common information and bold text

verdicts.trueWording: Dr Simon, post #8, names the Dragonlance boxed text
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the page: 'I think my favourite worst offender is the very first piece of boxed text that you meet in the Dragonlance series; "The air surges fierce and sweet..."'. But it is post #8 by Dr Simon (Jul 18, 2013), not delericho. delericho's post #7 (Jul 16, 2013) is the bullet-point-instead-of-boxed-text advice; Dr Simon's post opens by addressing 'Delericho,' which is the likely source of the mix-up. Claim sentence itself is otherwise fully supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The Forest Oracle's 'men who are neither tarrying nor running'
verdicts.note: Dausuul, post #5, Jul 15 2013: 'Now, this isn't awful boxed text--nothing like the infamous bit from "The Forest Oracle" with the men who are neither tarrying nor running--but it can certainly be tightened up considerably.' Author, post number and 'infamous' framing all match.

verdicts.trueWording: avoid having rooms that are just one thing
verdicts.note: Alexandrian, 'Random GM Tip: Awesome Dungeon Rooms' (19 Jan 2022): 'our key tip today for making awesome dungeon rooms is to avoid having rooms that are just one thing*'. Quote verbatim; the rule is stated as the article's key tip for a keyed room.

verdicts.trueWording: include at least three interactive elements
verdicts.note: Same article: 'A good rule of thumb here is to include at least three interactive elements (i.e., things that require or reward the players for doing more than just looking at them).' Both limbs -- the number three and 'more than looking' -- are on the page verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: one flavorful thing without a significant interaction
verdicts.note: Same article, the footnote marked by the asterisk: 'The exception are empty rooms. In my dungeons, empty rooms are rarely truly empty (in the sense of being barren and featureless). Instead, "empty" rooms commonly feature one flavorful thing which does not have a significant interaction. ("Cool mural! Okay, let's go left.")'. 'Barren and featureless' and 'footnote' both match.

verdicts.trueWording: note crucial details buried in the middle of a paragraph
verdicts.note: 'How to Prep a Module - Part 2' (28 Jul 2021), under the heading PREPPING PUBLISHED DUNGEONS: 'I usually won't waste a lot of time bringing them up to code... I find it more effective to occasionally make note of particularly crucial details that are essential to the adventure but buried in the middle of a paragraph, to make sure they don't get missed during play.' Quote verbatim and the section heading matches. Nuance: the page's own adverb is 'occasionally', set against 'usually won't' rewrite -- i.e. this is his standing light-touch repair rather than a per-room routine.

verdicts.trueWording: main text and glossary define the Influence action differently
verdicts.note: 'Review: Heroes of the Borderlands (D&D Starter Set 2025)' (16 Oct 2025): 'For example, in the main text the Influence action is defined as making a Charisma check to alter a creature's attitude. In the glossary, however, the Influence action is defined as making a monster do something you want and the monster's attitude is now a modifier on the check.' Quote verbatim; both definitions are located in the set's Play Guide, which the review has just called a glossary-based rulebook.

verdicts.trueWording: boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences
verdicts.note: GM Lent, post #31, Apr 5 2025: 'I remember reading a suggestion somewhere that boxed text shouldn't be more than two sentences, and should focus on what a character can physically sense when entering the room (what they see, feel, hear, etc). Any monsters or creatures in the room should get a mention too.' Author, post number, date, the recall framing, the sensing limb and the creatures limb all match.

el-remmen (listed as Moderator Emeritus), post #34, Apr 5 2025: 'I find it useful if written well and concisely. 3 to 5 sentences at most and then other details listed to be shared if the party looks closer/investigates/interacts.' Quote verbatim; the held-back-detail limb is the second half of the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: hates plain descriptors and boxes of unevocative keyterms
verdicts.note: Shardstone, post #32, Apr 5 2025: 'I love read aloud text in my adventures... I really hate adventures that have very plain descriptors or that have a box of simple keyterms that aren't evocative.' Quote verbatim; the pro-prose limb and the bullet-keyword alternative are both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: 'off to the side' changes when you enter another door
verdicts.note: Shiroiken, quoted in full inside Lanefan's post #36 (Apr 5 2025): 'I personally dislike the cardinal directions because the party may not know the cardinal direction... Personally I prefer vague descriptions when dealing with relative locations. "Off to the side" and "nearby" are typically adequate.' Lanefan replies: 'To me that's exactly the problem: "off to the side" when coming in one door might be "across the room" when coming in another or "against one wall" if coming up through a trap door in the floor.' Both halves of the claim, and the 'quoted post' page note, check out.

verdicts.trueWording: basic room description first, then monsters, minor details after the fight
verdicts.note: DragonLancer, quoted inside MarkB's post #39 (Apr 5 2025): 'The author will describe the minutia in a room but never mention any monsters or at the very least, put that in last. They would rather have a basic description of a scene or room, then the monsters, and any relevant minor details after a fight or encounter.' Quote is verbatim and the deferred-minor-detail limb is exact. But the ordering limb inverts him: he wants a basic room description BEFORE the creatures, with only the minutia held back -- not the creatures named first.

verdicts.trueWording: modules' language differs from his GMing voice; reading flags a clue
verdicts.note: humble minion, post #4, Jul 12 2020: 'I try not to use it, because the way modules are written is very different to my normal use of language when I'm GMing. Reading out a chunk of boxed text is basically equivalent to waving a "this location/NPC is A Clue to the plot, pay lots of attention to it" flag in front of my players' eyes.' Quote verbatim; both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: it turns the DM into a TextToSpeech bot
verdicts.note: oriaxx77, the thread's opening post #1, Jul 12 2020: 'I am from eastern Europe where not everyone speaks English. Maybe that is why. The read aloud seems weird and it turns the DM into a TextToSpeech bot.' Opening-poster, eastern-Europe and speech-synthesiser limbs all verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: divided between common information and bold text players aren't meant to know
verdicts.note: Age of Dusk, '[Review] T1 The Village of Hommlet (AD&D); Foreshadow', posted July 31 2021 by Prince: 'The village itself is helpfully divided between common information and bold text that the players are not meant to know and that can only be discovered by careful investigation.' It sits in the paragraph beginning 'There are the usual early TSR bugaboos with the module', exactly as the page field says.
